beats.narration: Begin by framing Course Scope & Audience as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. This class is restricted to students with at least 4th year standing COMPSCI-BS or COMPSCI-2M Contact Hours: Lecture 3 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: Writing Intensive: Program Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer. Consider this worked case: A senior software engineer preparing a technical report for a research grant must follow this course's formatting and ethical guidelines. On screen, display a course catalog excerpt highlighting the Writing Intensive designation, fourth-year restriction, and lecture contact hours. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Course Scope & Audience
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a course catalog excerpt highlighting the Writing Intensive designation, fourth-year restriction, and lecture contact hours.

beats.narration: Now define Document Types in Computer Science precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Topics include the different forms of writing in computer science (books, theses, journal articles, technical reports, manuscripts, etc. Consider this worked case: A thesis requires a comprehensive literature review and methodology section, whereas a journal article emphasizes novel findings and concise results. On screen, show a comparison chart listing document types alongside their primary purposes and typical audience expectations. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.
beats.title: Document Types in Computer Science
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a comparison chart listing document types alongside their primary purposes and typical audience expectations.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Algorithm Documentation Standards operates in a concrete sequence. Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Consider this worked case: A developer documenting a sorting algorithm must explicitly state preconditions, postconditions, and time complexity before presenting pseudocode. On screen, display a template for algorithm documentation with labeled sections for inputs, outputs, correctness arguments, and asymptotic analysis. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Algorithm Documentation Standards
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a template for algorithm documentation with labeled sections for inputs, outputs, correctness arguments, and asymptotic analysis.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Asymptotic Notation & Resource Bounds and make the decision criteria explicit. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. Consider this worked case: Using Big-O notation, a developer can demonstrate that a divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm outperforms a linear scan for large datasets. On screen, graph input size against resource consumption using logarithmic scales to illustrate linear, logarithmic, and polynomial growth patterns. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Asymptotic Notation & Resource Bounds
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Graph input size against resource consumption using logarithmic scales to illustrate linear, logarithmic, and polynomial growth patterns.

beats.narration: Apply Data Structure Representation Choices to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible. Consider this worked case: Selecting a hash table over a linked list for key-value storage reduces lookup time from O(n) to O(1) on average, which must be explicitly noted in technical documentation. On screen, show side-by-side diagrams of a hash table and a linked list with annotated operation costs and collision handling strategies. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Data Structure Representation Choices
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show side-by-side diagrams of a hash table and a linked list with annotated operation costs and collision handling strategies.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Graph Algorithms & Traversal, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Consider this worked case: A network engineer documenting a shortest path algorithm must explain how adjacency matrices or adjacency lists represent the graph structure. On screen, render a directed graph with labeled vertices and edges, highlighting traversal paths and connectivity metrics. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Graph Algorithms & Traversal
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Render a directed graph with labeled vertices and edges, highlighting traversal paths and connectivity metrics.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Dynamic Programming & Overlapping Subproblems with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems. Consider this worked case: A developer documenting a Fibonacci sequence calculator must show how memoization tables store intermediate results to reduce time complexity. On screen, display a memoization table filling process with arrows indicating subproblem reuse and final solution assembly. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Dynamic Programming & Overlapping Subproblems
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a memoization table filling process with arrows indicating subproblem reuse and final solution assembly.

Consider this worked case: A bar chart comparing algorithm runtimes must include axis labels, a legend, and consistent units to accurately convey performance differences. On screen, show a before-and-after comparison of a poorly formatted chart versus a professionally formatted technical figure with clear axes and legends. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.

beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a before-and-after comparison of a poorly formatted chart versus a professionally formatted technical figure with clear axes and legends.

beats.narration: Connect Teamwork & Peer Review Practices to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. This course focuses on developing and improving verbal and written communication skills specific to the discipline of computer science. Consider this worked case: A research group uses a standardized peer review checklist to evaluate algorithm correctness, clarity of notation, and adherence to formatting standards before submission. On screen, display a peer review checklist template with categories for correctness, readability, formatting, and ethical compliance. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Teamwork & Peer Review Practices
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a peer review checklist template with categories for correctness, readability, formatting, and ethical compliance.

beats.narration: Finish with Ethical & Professional Considerations as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Consider this worked case: A developer documenting a machine learning model must disclose training data sources, potential biases, and limitations to maintain professional integrity. On screen, show a professional communication checklist highlighting ethical disclosure, authorship attribution, and data privacy compliance. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.

beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a professional communication checklist highlighting ethical disclosure, authorship attribution, and data privacy compliance.

sources.author: MIT OpenCourseWare
sources.excerpt: Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems. Core methods include sorting, hashing, trees, graphs, shortest paths, and dynamic programming. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space.
sources.title: MIT OpenCourseWare Introduction to Algorithms

sources.author: OpenDSA Project
sources.excerpt: OpenDSA presents data structures and algorithms through executable visualizations and exercises. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Stacks use last-in, first-out access, while queues use first-in, first-out access. Trees represent hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms. Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible.
